CMPE 249 · Agentic Autonomy and Safety and Evaluation

Which perception tool should a driving planner call, and when?

A learned selector that looks at the candidate trajectories, tested on fresh seeds

Eshan Chawla and Max Dokukin

Project CASS-VLA, Phase 1 (PlanDiscrim)

The problem

The question: cheaper perception checks, without losing safety

Our professor narrowed the project to one question:

Given candidate trajectories and an ambiguous scene, can a selector choose the one perception query that matters most? It should match always-on checking at far lower cost, and beat uncertainty-based selection at the same budget.

Calling every perception tool on every decision is costly. It can also hurt: extra evidence sometimes contradicts a correct judgment.

Tool-using driving agents such as DriveAgent-R1 decide from the scene alone. Plan-value gates exist, but we found none that chooses among perception tools from how the candidates differ.

Our bet: a scene can be uncertain in ways that do not matter for the choice at hand. The candidates show which uncertainty matters.

Two rivals: always-on (the cost reference) and a generic uncertainty trigger (the equal-budget rival).

CMPE 249 · CASS-VLA · 2

Setup

Setup: three tools, a few candidates, a call budget

Simulator

MetaDrive, six scenario families: ambiguous light, lane blockage, lead brake or cut-in, merge, occluded cross traffic, occluded pedestrian.

Up to 6 candidate maneuvers per decision (K), over a 5 s horizon: keep, keep fast, decelerate, stop, change left, change right. A lane change exists only when the lane does.

Labels come from simulator ground truth (the oracle).

Tools and noise

Three simulated tools: ROI check, depth, geometric collision check.

Each tool is noisy. We test three noise levels: low, mid and high.

A tool result goes to the ranker, which picks the top candidate again.

Budget

The selector makes at most one call per decision, or none.

Budget = calls per decision. A budget of 0.6 means 60% of decisions get one call.

Always-on calls all 3 tools every time: 3 calls per decision.

Accuracy: the ranker’s top candidate equals the oracle’s best candidate. Unsafe: the oracle labels the chosen candidate unsafe.

CMPE 249 · CASS-VLA · 3

Method

Method: pick the tool from the candidates

Scene and candidates

ego state, hazards, K trajectories

→

Candidate features

which candidate is on top, how it differs from the runner-up, safety and occlusion

→

Small MLP

32 hidden units, one output per tool

→

Predicted gain per tool

ROI, depth, collision

→

Call or abstain

call the best tool only if its gain is above 0

Frozen MLP (first version)

Trained to predict the gain of each tool, clipped at 0. It never learns that a call can hurt.

Calls are ranked by score and spent up to the budget. It calls too much at high budgets.

Signed-gain abstain (primary)

Same network with a linear output. It is trained on the signed expected gain, so negative gains are visible.

It calls only when the best predicted gain is above 0, and it picks that tool. No extra threshold to tune.

Why it works

What drives it: knowing which candidate is on top

Candidates beat scene. A model with candidate features beats the scene-only model by 0.011 to 0.026 in every val and test cell.

It holds on fresh seeds. Signed minus signed scene-only: +0.017, +0.023, +0.026 (low, mid, high), all CIs above 0.

The identity of the top candidate costs the most when shuffled. Divergence features cost less (permutation importance, no ablation run).

Divergence features (when and how the top two candidates part ways) add a smaller share. The time of divergence is the strongest one.

Biggest gains over scene-only: lane blockage and occluded pedestrian.

Failure analysis

Where it goes wrong: late calls and wrong decisions

Harm rate at budget 0.1SignedFrozen
Low noise0.0000.005
Mid noise0.0020.037
High noise0.0020.083

Harm rate: share of made calls whose tool has negative expected gain. Second final test. The uncertainty margin trigger at mid noise: 0.388.

Drop in accuracy after budget 0.65, frozen vs signed: 0.027 vs 0.001, 0.043 vs 0.001, 0.058 vs 0.000 (low, mid, high).

Late calls hurt. On val and test, calls ranked past 65% are harmful 26% to 46% of the time, yet hold only 4% to 10% of the gain.

Wrong decision beats wrong tool. 55% to 76% of the gap to the ceiling is calling the wrong decisions.

Depth collapse. At mid noise the frozen model predicts depth on 1,514 of 2,222 val decisions. It predicts collision on 130, where collision is best on 272.

CMPE 249 · CASS-VLA · 13

Phase 5 · vision-language features

VLM features: a small gain, about half beyond scene family

32 PCA dimensions of Qwen3.5-9B image features are added to the geometry features.

Frozen MLP: +0.005 to +0.010 mean accuracy, positive for all three init seeds in every cell.

Signed model, val and test: +0.008 to +0.015 over geometry-only on the same rows, all CIs above 0 (exploratory).

Controls (frozen MLP, one run per cell, no CIs): shuffled features remove the gain. A scene-family code alone recovers 49% of it, so about half is information beyond family.

Q1: passes

Signed plus VLM minus signed, second final test, mean accuracy (95% CI):

Low: +0.0163 [0.0129, 0.0196]

Mid: +0.0115 [0.0084, 0.0149]

High: +0.0099 [0.0073, 0.0125]

The first final test had no frames, so it has no VLM result. The shuffle and family controls were not rerun on the signed model, so extra capacity (71 vs 39 inputs) is not ruled out.

CMPE 249 · CASS-VLA · 14

Limits

Limits: what these numbers do and do not show

Open loop, not driving. Accuracy is top-1 agreement with the oracle’s best candidate. We never ran the chosen candidate in the simulator.

"Unsafe" is a label, not a collision. It is the oracle’s unsafe label on the chosen candidate. No closed-loop collision rate exists.

Simulated tools. A call is a noisy simulated tool, not a real perception model. Always-on merges all three outputs and is not a VLM verifier.

One simulator and one generator. MetaDrive, six families, one noise model. Seeds differ across splits, but the generator does not.

Multiple comparisons. Four primary hypotheses, no correction. About a dozen variants were tried on val and test before one was pre-registered.

The 0.6 budget was chosen post hoc from the first final test. The second test used fresh seeds, but the budget was not blind to the first.

VLM controls have no CIs and were not repeated on the signed model.

CMPE 249 · CASS-VLA · 15

What we would do next

Next steps

Closed loop. Run the selected candidate in MetaDrive and count collisions at about 0.6 calls per decision, against always-on. This is the main gap.

Control the VLM gain. Q1 passed, but repeat the shuffle and family controls on the signed model, since capacity is not ruled out.

Choose the tool better. The signed model stops calling at the right places, but picks the best tool less often. Offsets and thresholds gave nothing, so try a two-stage model.

Put CIs on unsafe-rate differences at a budget fixed in advance. Only accuracy has CIs in the first test.

Look at lead_brake_cutin. It is the largest family, has the lowest ceiling and is where simple triggers can win.

Test with real tools and a second simulator.

CMPE 249 · CASS-VLA · 16

Take-away

Summary

A selector that sees the candidate trajectories beats the generic uncertainty trigger by about 0.07 to 0.10 mean accuracy, and beats a scene-only selector.

The signed-gain version stops calling when no tool is predicted to help, so the curve no longer falls at high budgets. It confirmed on fresh seeds at mid and high noise.

At 0.6 calls per decision, 20% of always-on’s cost, it is within the 0.01 accuracy margin of always-on and safer at all three noise levels. Unsafe rate is −0.013, −0.025 and −0.034 relative to always-on.

Adding VLM image features to the signed model helps at all three noise levels (Q1, +0.010 to +0.016), though capacity is not ruled out.

The evidence is open loop with simulated tools. Closed-loop collisions are the next test.
